prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators and its experimental realisation in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: I moved my first preference from B001 to B039 after reading the other ballots. Topological insulators are the one candidate that five members placed in their top three and that all eight ranked. The discovery is original and conceptually clean: a classification of electronic phases by band-structure invariants rather than broken symmetry, with protected edge and surface states. It follows a clear theory-to-experiment chain, from the Kane-Mele proposal to the Molenkamp-group observation in HgTe wells. It has been confirmed over almost two decades by transport, photoemission and scanning probes in several material families, so the interpretation is stable. As an experimentalist in materials physics I also value that the work depends on interfaces and quantum-well structures that had to be grown and characterised with atomic precision, which is why the Molenkamp part of the credit matters and is more than a decoration on a theory prize. It also complements the 2016 prize for topological phases of matter without duplicating it, since time-reversal-invariant systems were not covered there. If the criterion is a discovery or invention with identifiable originators, this is the strongest combined case on the list.
statement.case_against: The credited trio does not exhaust the credit. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the HgTe prediction that directly enabled Molenkamp's experiment, and the three-dimensional topological insulators (Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents, Hasan and others) are a large part of why the field became a materials-science field. A prize framed on the 2D quantum spin Hall effect is therefore defensible but leaves a visible omission, and a prize framed on topological insulators in general would need names that are not in the supplied credit. I cannot settle priority from the file, and I rely on recollection for these points. A second reservation is that practical applications remain limited, so the case rests on conceptual and materials impact.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked B039 first but flagged that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and the 3D work, complicate fairness, and that the committee must not split this field across two candidates.
responses.response: I agree that the omission is the real weakness and that I cannot repair it with the supplied names. I would answer it in the citation rather than in the head count. If the citation is anchored on the quantum spin Hall effect and its observation in HgTe, the Kane-Mele and Molenkamp credit is coherent and the omitted HgTe theorists are a recognised cost, not a hidden one. I do not think the 2D versus 3D question is resolved by adding names, and I would not widen the prize to cover 3D materials. I share your caution about splitting the field, so I would not support B039 together with another topological candidate.

responses.point: Johansson ranked B039 first and B022 second, and placed B001 fourth with the reservation that the quantum cascade laser may be seen as engineering and that Kazarinov-Suris and the Bell Labs co-authors are unresolved.
responses.response: This is a fair challenge to my own opening first choice and it moved me. The quantum cascade laser is a real invention in the statutory sense, but my attribution confidence was lower than my enthusiasm. Sirtori, Sivco, Hutchinson and the 1971 Kazarinov-Suris proposal are outside the names we can credit, and I recalled the original author list from memory only. Only two members ranked B001 at all, so I do not think I can argue it is the committee's lead candidate. I still disagree that it is merely engineering. The unipolar intersubband design is a physical concept realised through epitaxial interface control. I would keep it as an alternative rather than drop it.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked the optical lattice clock first and called B039 a natural complement to the 2016 topological-phase prize, extending it to time-reversal-invariant systems, while noting that omitted theorists make any three-person configuration contestable.
responses.response: I agree with the complement argument and use it in my case for B039. I also take her point that the omissions make every configuration here contestable, which is why I would not over-weight the lack of a clean credit list as a reason to prefer clocks. On B022, I still rank it fourth, not first. The clean two-name credit is a strength. But the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for single-quantum-system control sit close to it, and the redefinition of the second has not taken place. I regard it as a strong alternative and not as a clearly better lead.

responses.point: Kroll ranked the optical lattice clock first, arguing that Katori and Ye give a clean two-person allocation, multiple independent laboratories have reproduced it, and timing is excellent, while ranking B039 only eighth.
responses.response: I accept the clock attribution is cleaner than topological insulators, and that is a legitimate point for a committee that must name people. Where I disagree is on weight: his eighth place for B039 treats the omitted-theorist problem as decisive, whereas seven members placed it in their top five. A tidy credit list should not substitute for the size of the scientific change. Clocks improved a measurement by orders of magnitude, which is a major advance. Topological insulators changed how a community classifies electronic states. I would ask him whether a prize on B022 is better timed after the redefinition of the second, since that would settle a maturity milestone he himself raises.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, ranked IceCube neutrino astronomy first but conceded that a single-laureate award is a thin summary of a collaboration-scale discovery and that earlier pioneers cannot be represented.
responses.response: I appreciate the candour, and it is the reason I will not support B003 as a lead. The scientific case for opening neutrino astronomy is strong, but a one-name prize for a large collaboration, with AMANDA, DUMAND and Baikal pioneers outside the list, runs against the committee's duty to identify the people responsible for the original work. I would be willing to revisit it if the committee found a defensible credited set, but with the file as supplied I cannot.

uncertainties: Whether the prize should be framed on the 2D quantum spin Hall effect or on topological insulators more generally, and how the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and 3D contributions would be treated.
My recollection of the original quantum cascade laser author list and of the Kazarinov-Suris priority has not been verified from the supplied material.
Whether the committee regards the 2016 prize as close enough to B039 to count against novelty.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B039, B001 or B022 from my profile: I have no documented tie to Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Capasso, Faist, Cho, Katori or Ye. I should disclose that Göran Johansson is also at Chalmers, though he is a colleague on the committee and not a candidate. My interest in epitaxial interfaces and electron microscopy is field proximity and not a personal connection.
